Bonneville whitefish (Prosopium spilonotus) attains a maximum recorded total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], placing it among the larger members of the genus. This ultimate size is reached only after many years of slow, cold-water growth in the deep, oligotrophic lakes of the Bonneville Basin. Field surveys of spawning aggregations indicate that individuals first become reproductively active at a considerably smaller size, with the total length at puberty measured at 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm]. This pronounced size differential between the onset of maturity and the maximum achievable length reflects a life-history strategy common to many lacustrine coregonids, where early maturation is favored under conditions of high adult mortality or unpredictable recruitment. The transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to a mature, spawning adult is marked by this 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm] threshold, after which individuals redirect energy from somatic growth toward gamete production. Unlike some congeneric species that delay maturation further, Bonneville whitefish appears to prioritize early breeding, a pattern confirmed by otolith-based age-length keys from Bear Lake.

Hatchling mass was estimated from the average diameter of fertilized ova, which for the closely related round whitefish (Prosopium cylindraceum) ranges from 1.9 to 2.4 mm, yielding a calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0048 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0048 grams]. This minute body mass at emergence from the gravel substrate reflects the high fecundity characteristic of the genus, as females produce thousands of small, yolk-rich demersal eggs during autumn spawning runs. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or alevin, measures only a few millimeters and relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first several weeks of life. During this lecithotrophic phase, the larva remains hidden within the interstitial spaces of the spawning gravel, where it undergoes organogenesis and pigmentation before initiating exogenous feeding. The small birth mass of 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams] is consistent with values reported for other small-egged coregonids and imposes a narrow window for successful first feeding, as the yolk reserves are depleted within a few weeks at typical incubation temperatures.

Maximum adult body mass has been estimated from length-weight regressions developed for Bear Lake populations, yielding an ultimate wet weight of 683 grams [Wwi = 683 grams] for a fish of 45 cm total length. This value is derived from field-collected specimens spanning the full size range and conforms to the relationship W = 0.00457 L^3.13, a curve typical of deep-bodied lacustrine salmonids. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty for a fish of 18 cm total length is calculated to be 38.8 grams [Wwp = 38.8 grams], representing only about 5.7 percent of the ultimate body mass. This marked disparity between mass at maturity and asymptotic mass suggests that Bonneville whitefish invests heavily in post-maturation somatic growth, a strategy that may buffer against interannual variability in food availability. The slope of the length-weight relationship, with an exponent exceeding three, indicates that larger fish become progressively more rotund, likely reflecting the accumulation of lipid reserves in the visceral cavity prior to winter spawning. These lipid stores are critical for sustaining the energetically demanding migration to shallow, rocky spawning areas.

Longevity records for Bonneville whitefish, based on otolith annuli from a long-term mark-recapture study in Bear Lake, indicate a maximum lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This extended lifespan is typical of cold-stenothermal coregonids inhabiting deep, thermally stable lakes where metabolic rates are low and somatic growth is slow but sustained over many decades. The 14-year maximum (14 years) [am = 14 years] contrasts with shorter-lived populations of the same genus from warmer, more productive systems, emphasizing the strong influence of temperature on aging at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. At 4 °C [T = 4 °C], annual metabolic expenditure is minimized, allowing individuals to allocate energy to both reproduction and growth without incurring the accelerated senescence observed in warmer-water fish. Field records from tagged individuals show that many adults survive to spawn repeatedly over a decade, with the oldest confirmed specimen aged at 14 years [am = 14 years] at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This iteroparous strategy is well suited to the stable but low-productivity environment of Bear Lake.

The reproductive schedule of Bonneville whitefish is tightly coupled to the cold thermal regime of its native habitat. Spawning occurs in late autumn, when water temperatures drop below 8 °C, and females deposit their adhesive eggs over clean gravel substrates in shallow littoral zones. The resulting fertilized ova then incubate over winter at temperatures near 4 °C [T = 4 °C], a period that extends embryonic development and yolk absorption. Because the lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years] is achieved only at these persistently cold temperatures, any warming trend could compress the reproductive window and reduce the number of spawning opportunities per individual at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. Comparative data from related Prosopium species suggest that even modest increases in mean annual temperature can shift the timing of spawning and reduce egg survival, highlighting the vulnerability of this relict lineage to climate change. The long generation time implied by a 14-year lifespan (14 years) [am = 14 years] further limits the species' capacity for rapid adaptation, making the preservation of its current thermal environment a priority for fisheries managers at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C].
